statement: Three screen-level uses of Windows APIs exist: the main window hides its horizontal scrollbar through a user32 call, the main window's load asks kernel32 (via the edition check) whether Group Policy exists, and the ADMX download dialog enables token privileges through advapi32. Everything else reaches the registry only indirectly, by asking a policy loader to open, save or close a source.

evidence.shows: Main window calls ShowScrollBar on the setting info panel
Main window load calls HasGroupPolicyInfrastructure
That check reads the Windows edition through kernel32
Download dialog enables take-ownership and restore privileges
Dialog builds policy loaders for registry, file, user GPO and hive choices

statement: The contract with Windows is by name: native functions are named with their DLL (for example RegLoadKeyW in advapi32), and registry locations are text paths such as Software\Policies under the machine or user root. Roots accepted by text are HKCU, HKU and HKLM, short or long form. Three lowercase branches (software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies, system\currentcontrolset\policies) are fixed in code, but only to scope which keys a policy-file difference tracks; other registry paths are still readable and writable.

evidence.shows: Hive load and unload declared with DLL name and wide-string arguments
Typed registry path is split at the first backslash and its root name matched
PolicyKeys lists the three branches, which only limit what ApplyDifference tracks

statement: Registry data is shaped in code: policy values are typed numeric, string, multi-string or binary and passed through one policy-source interface, with registry, policy file and hive-file implementations. The registry implementation converts unsigned 32/64-bit numbers to the registry's signed form on write and back on read; native structs are defined for token privileges.

evidence.shows: Single interface for reading and writing policy values
RegistryPolicyProxy.SetValue reinterprets unsigned numbers as signed before writing
GetValue reinterprets signed numbers back to unsigned
Two native structures for privilege adjustment

statement: Nothing in the project changes which Windows API code exists: all native declarations are compiled unconditionally in every build. The only conditional compilation is the generated _MyType check in the settings designer; no #If or #Const touches registry or Win32 code, and the project defines no custom constants. Debug and Release differ only in debug, trace and optimisation flags, and the manifest is embedded in all builds.

evidence.shows: Debug and Release set only debug, trace, optimisation and output flags, no custom constants
The only #If in the source is this generated _MyType check (also line 43)
Application manifest is set unconditionally
Declarations carry no conditional compilation

statement: When the user presses start, the ADMX download fetches a Microsoft installer package from a fixed https address with WebClient, with no hash, signature or publisher check, and the app allows TLS 1.0 and 1.1 as well as 1.2 for it. It is unpacked with msiexec /a (an administrative extract, not an install) and only the ADMX/ADML files are moved into the policy folder the app takes ownership of as administrator. A tampered package, for example through a downgraded connection, would put attacker-chosen policy definition files there; reach is this download only.

evidence.shows: Fixed https download address on a Microsoft host
SecurityProtocol set to Tls, Tls11 and Tls12 at main window load
Whole download runs only from the start button click
Package downloaded and extracted with msiexec /a, no verification
Administrator takes ownership of the destination, then extracted files are moved in
